hints: Look at all three statements as Group 2 trends going down from magnesium to calcium, think size, charge density and ease of losing electrons.
Remember that the smaller $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion polarises the carbonate ion more strongly, so $\text{MgCO}_3$ breaks down more easily on heating.
Check solubility of hydroxides and reducing power both increase down the group, so see which combination of statements that leaves you with.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 - thermal decomposition**

Think of the metal ion pulling on the electrons of the carbonate ion. The smaller ion pulls harder and weakens it.

$$\text{MCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$$
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ with the same charge, so it has higher charge density and greater polarising power. It distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion more, so $\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes at a lower temperature. Statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2 - solubility of hydroxides**

For Group 2, hydroxides get more soluble as you go down the group. This is the opposite trend to sulfates.

$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is almost insoluble in water, while $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble and gives limewater. So calcium hydroxide is more soluble than magnesium hydroxide. Statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3 - reducing strength**

A reducing agent loses electrons itself. For metals, this means $\text{M} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+} + 2e^-$.

Going down Group 2, atomic size increases and first and second ionisation energies decrease, so electrons are lost more easily. Calcium is more reactive and a stronger reducing agent than magnesium. Statement 3 is correct.

Since 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, select the option for all three.

options.A: Correct. All three statements are true. MgCO3 decomposes more easily due to greater polarisation by Mg2+, Ca(OH)2 is more soluble than Mg(OH)2 down the group trend, and Ca is a stronger reducing agent due to lower ionisation energies.
options.B: Incorrect. This option omits one of the true statements. Students sometimes doubt statement 3 because magnesium is already very reactive, but reactivity and reducing power do increase from Mg to Ca.
options.C: Incorrect. This option omits statement 1. Students sometimes reverse the carbonate stability trend, thinking larger cations are less stable, but stability increases down the group so MgCO3 decomposes lower.
options.D: Incorrect. This option includes only one or two statements. Students sometimes think Ca(OH)2 is insoluble like Mg(OH)2, but hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2.
